title: Spotting Child Sexual Exploitation (CSE)
blurb: How to recognise possible signs of child sexual exploitation, and how to report a concern safely to the Duty Manager.
siteNotes: Who the Duty Manager is on each shift and how to reach them, including late at night
Whether the venue has a named safeguarding lead and a written reporting route beyond the Duty Manager
Where concerns are recorded and who is allowed to see the record
legalNotes: From BHB-10MT-23. Safeguarding good practice; the trainer states no regulation.

CHECK: the trainer sends every concern to the Duty Manager, who decides what happens next. Confirm the venue has a named safeguarding lead and a clear route to the police (101) and children's services, so the Duty Manager is not left to decide alone.

CHECK: the trainer lists warning signs only in outline (adult booking a room with an anxious or controlled young person, secrecy, little control over money, phone or movements). Confirm they match current guidance, such as that from the police and the NSPCC, before relying on the list.
CHECK: the trainer says to keep concerns confidential. Confirm the venue also tells staff that confidentiality never stops a safeguarding report being passed to the Duty Manager or the police.

cards.title: Spotting Child Sexual Exploitation (CSE)
cards.body:
By the end of this session you can:
- explain what CSE is and why venues matter
- recognise warning signs
- report a concern safely, or call 999 if a child is in danger

cards.title: Our responsibility
cards.body:
As a hotel and events venue we have a real responsibility to help keep children safe. CSE is a form of abuse where a child is manipulated or coerced into sexual activity, sometimes in places just like ours.
> Being aware, and knowing what to do, can genuinely protect a young person.

cards.title: What to be alert to
cards.body: Be cautious about an adult booking a room with a child or young person who seems anxious, withdrawn, frightened or under the adult's control, particularly where there is an obvious age gap.

items.title: Anxious or withdrawn
items.text: Frightened, or seems under the adult's control

items.title: Out of place
items.text: An obvious age gap, or a young person who seems out of place

items.title: Little control
items.text: Over their own money, phone or movements

items.title: Secrecy
items.text: Attempts to keep a booking secret

cards.title: Notice, note, report
cards.body: Trust your instinct, but do not investigate or confront anyone yourself. That could put you or the young person at greater risk.

items.title: Note
items.text: Write down what you actually saw or heard

items.title: Report
items.text: Tell the Duty Manager, who decides what happens

cards.title: Do not investigate or confront
cards.body: Quietly note what you have seen, report it, and leave the decision to the Duty Manager.

cards.title: 999, and confidentiality
cards.body:
If a child appears to be in immediate danger, call 999 without delay. Keep any concern confidential and share it only with those who genuinely need to know.
> You do not need to be certain. You just need to notice and speak up. The child's welfare always comes first.

cards.title: Remember
cards.body:
- CSE is abuse, and venues like ours can be where it happens.
- Warning signs: a young person who seems controlled, frightened, secretive or without control of money, phone or movements.
- Never investigate or confront. Note what you saw and tell the Duty Manager.
- Child in immediate danger: call 999 without delay.
- You do not need to be certain. Speak up. Welfare comes first.

cards.q: As a hotel and venue we have a responsibility to help keep children safe.
cards.why: Venues like ours can be places where exploitation happens, so we share responsibility for noticing it.

cards.q: If you have a CSE concern, you should…
options: Note it and tell the Duty Manager
cards.why: Quietly note what you actually saw or heard and report it to the Duty Manager, who decides what happens next.

cards.q: You should confront the adult directly if you're suspicious.
cards.why: Never confront or investigate. It could put you or the young person at greater risk.

cards.q: If a child appears to be in immediate danger, what should you do?
options: Tell the Duty Manager at the end of the shift
Knock on the room door to check
Note it down and keep watching

cards.q: Which could be a warning sign?
options: A child who seems happy and relaxed
A young person with no say over money or phone
A teenager asking for extra towels
cards.why: A young person with little control over their own money, phone or movements may be under someone's control.

cards.q: You need to be completely certain before reporting a concern.
cards.why: You do not need to be certain or have all the answers. You just need to notice and speak up.

cards.q: Who is responsible for deciding what happens after you report a concern?
options: You, once you have gathered more evidence
cards.why: You report it to the Duty Manager, who is responsible for deciding what happens next.

cards.q: If something doesn't feel right, that instinct is worth acting on.
cards.why: Trust that instinct, and report it rather than investigating.
Keep any concern confidential and share it only with those who genuinely need to know.

cards.q: The child's welfare always comes first.
cards.why: Whatever else is going on, the child's welfare always comes first.
